power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

report: Reporting *p* values imprecisely (e.g., *p* < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in *p* value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., *p* = .032) unless *p* values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use *p* < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., "decreased at the *p* < .05 significance threshold").

```{r}
#| echo: false


# table data --------------------------------------
table <- structure(list("P-Value" = "ps ≤ .040", Text = "Women were more likely than men to endorse situationships as dragging on without progression, being neither casual enough to feel meaningless nor serious enough to feel secure, involving emotional confusion or disagreement about the nature of the connection, and characterised by mixed signals (adjusted ps ≤ .040)."), row.names = c(NA, 
-1L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame"))

# display table -----------------------------------
metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 2, FALSE)
```

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} The APA manual states: Report exact *p* values (e.g., *p* = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report *p* values less than .001 as *p* < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a *p* value meta-analysis), so report *p* values with three digits. text.text: Situationships are an emerging relationship type, yet quantitative research remains limited.
Here we examined situationship characteristics and experiences, using sex and sociosexuality as theoretically relevant starting points for understanding individual variation.

We conducted an exploratory, cross-sectional survey of 390 adults (68% women; M age = 27.41 years, SD = 8.66) from 48 countries who reported on current, or emotionally significant past, situationships.
Participants endorsed proposed situationship characteristics and provided their own open-ended definitions which underwent structured content coding.
These analyses informed a working definition of situationships as intimate, relationship-like connections lacking clarity about commitment, relationship status, or future trajectory.
Although 56% of participants entered situationships hoping for a relationship, and 55% assumed sexual exclusivity, only 9% of reported past situationships progressed to a committed relationship.
Compared with men, women more often emphasised ambiguity in their definitions, perceived greater long-term potential, and expressed stronger hopes for commitment.
They also more strongly agreed that they would feel betrayed if their situationship partner saw other people.
Relative to the reference sample, both sexes reported more unrestricted sociosexual behaviour, whereas women reported more restricted sociosexual attitudes.
This pattern raises questions about incongruence between women's sexual experiences and preferences, with potential implications for wellbeing.
The observed sex differences also motivate future research to examine whether divergent mating goals between partners shape situationship experiences.
The term "situationship" has gained prominence in modern dating.
In popular usage, it describes connections involving emotional and sexual intimacy but lacking clear commitment or defined relational roles (Battle, 2023).
text.formatted: In popular usage, it describes connections involving emotional and sexual intimacy but lacking clear commitment or defined relational roles <ref type="bibr" target="#b0">(Battle, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Tinder reported a 49% increase in members adding the term to their dating profiles in 2022 (Tinder, 2022).
text.formatted: Tinder reported a 49% increase in members adding the term to their dating profiles in 2022 <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Tinder, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In 2023, Oxford shortlisted it for Word of the Year, defining it as "a romantic or sexual relationship that is not considered to be formal or established" (Oxford University Press, 2023).
A YouGov survey found that half of Americans aged 18-34 had experienced one (Shah, 2024).
text.formatted: A YouGov survey found that half of Americans aged 18-34 had experienced one <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Shah, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Despite their apparent prevalence, empirical research on situationships remains limited and often relies on narrow samples (e.g., Gibson, 2020). Langlais et al. (2024), for example, combined semi-structured interviews (N = 28) and an online survey (N = 261) about past situationships, highlighting romantic and sexual behaviours and time spent together alongside low commitment and ambiguous relationship labels.

(2024)</ref>, for example, combined semi-structured interviews (N = 28) and an online survey (N = 261) about past situationships, highlighting romantic and sexual behaviours and time spent together alongside low commitment and ambiguous relationship labels.

text.text: However, both samples consisted exclusively of students (age M = 20.80 and 19.89 years) and included only 8 and 32 men, respectively, limiting generalisability beyond students and leaving men's experiences less well characterised.
Although Langlais et al. (2024) offered an initial empirical definition of situationships, the relative prominence of individual features remains unclear.
text.formatted: Although <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Langlais et al. (2024)</ref> offered an initial empirical definition of situationships, the relative prominence of individual features remains unclear.

text.text: Studies have also often combined committed relationships, hookups, and friends-with-benefits relationships into one category, obscuring how situationships might differ from other casual relationship types (Langlais et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Studies have also often combined committed relationships, hookups, and friends-with-benefits relationships into one category, obscuring how situationships might differ from other casual relationship types <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Langlais et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Other casual sexual relationships have better-established definitions and distinguishing features (Wentland & Reissing, 2014).
text.formatted: Other casual sexual relationships have better-established definitions and distinguishing features <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Wentland & Reissing, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: One-night stands are brief sexual encounters typically without expectations of continuity (Campbell, 2008), whereas friends-with-benefits relationships combine friendship and sex outside an established romantic partnership (Bisson & Levine, 2009).

text.text: Clarifying how situationships differ from these relationships is therefore an important next step.
Individual differences in situationship experiences, including sex differences, also remain understudied.
Well-established sex differences in short-term mating orientation (Buss & Schmitt, 1993) raise questions about whether women and men understand and approach situationships differently.
text.formatted: Well-established sex differences in short-term mating orientation <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Buss & Schmitt, 1993</ref>) raise questions about whether women and men understand and approach situationships differently.

text.text: These relationships offer a context for examining how such differences manifest when sexual intimacy occurs but commitment remains uncertain.
Sociosexual orientation, or openness to uncommitted sex (Simpson & Gangestad, 1991), may also shape situationship experiences.
text.formatted: Sociosexual orientation, or openness to uncommitted sex <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Simpson & Gangestad, 1991)</ref>, may also shape situationship experiences.

text.text: Casual sex has been associated with better wellbeing among unrestricted individuals (Vrangalova & Ong, 2014), who may find various forms of relationships that offer sexual access satisfying (Thomas et al., 2024), potentially including situationships.
text.formatted: Casual sex has been associated with better wellbeing among unrestricted individuals <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Vrangalova & Ong, 2014)</ref>, who may find various forms of relationships that offer sexual access satisfying <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Thomas et al., 2024)</ref>, potentially including situationships.

text.text: For more restricted individuals, situationships may be less compatible with their relationship preferences, with potential implications for wellbeing and satisfaction.
To address these gaps, this exploratory study draws on a larger international sample of adults reporting current or past emotionally significant situationships.

We examine (1) how participants define situationships and distinguish them from related relationship forms; (2) sex differences in definitions, motivations, expectations, and experiences; and (3) participants' sociosexual orientation, including comparisons with previous research samples.
Alongside describing how situationships begin and develop, we aim to establish a working definition and provide a descriptive foundation for theory-driven hypothesis development and testing.
The study was an online, cross-sectional survey of adults with current or previous situationship experience.
Recruitment took place between May and October 2025.
Of 449 survey records, the analytic sample comprised 390 participants (n = 265 women), all of whom reported on a different-sex situationship.
Exclusions comprised 26 same-sex focal experiences, 30 attention-check failures, and four non-genuine responses; one participant met two criteria, yielding 59 unique exclusions.
Most identified as heterosexual (79.5%) or bisexual (19.5%) and 99.7% identified as cisgender.
Age was available for 389 participants (range = 18-75 years).
Men (M = 29.40, SD = 10.08) were significantly older than women (M = 26.47, SD = 7.74), Welch's t(195.64) = 2.87, p = .005, d = 0.34.
Participants described either a current (n = 117, 30.0%) or past (n = 273, 70.0%) situationship.
Participants came from 48 countries (one provided only a region).
Most lived in the USA (n = 134, 34.4%), UK (n = 73, 18.7%), Canada (n = 33, 8.5%), or Australia (n = 22, 5.6%).
The most common ethnicity was White (n = 247, 63.3%), followed by Asian (n = 54, 13.8%), and Hispanic/Latino (n = 41, 10.5%).
Most had experienced a committed relationship before (n = 321, 82.3%).
See Supplementary Table S1 for full demographic and relationship characteristics.
text.formatted: See Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_0">S1</ref> for full demographic and relationship characteristics.

text.text: Participants were recruited through social media, including X, TikTok, and Reddit, and campus posters.
The survey was administered using Jisc Online Surveys.
Recruitment and participant information described situationships as "relationships that exist between casual dating and committed partnerships" that "typically lack clear labels or commitment".
Individuals could participate if this description matched an experience, even if they had not previously called it a situationship.
Participants completed a select-all-that-apply checklist asking what distinguished situationships from friends-with-benefits relationships, casual dating, or hookups.
The checklist contained ten statements and an "Other" option, followed by an open-ended question asking participants to define a situationship in their own words.
These questions assessed perceptions of the category.
A separate yes/no item assessed sexual involvement in the focal situationship without specifying a particular sexual act.
Participants reported where they met their focal partner, who initiated the connection, and the interval between their previous breakup and the situationship's beginning.
Separate questions assessed the duration of past and current situationships using five categories ranging from less than one month to 12 months or longer.
Participants indicated whether the situationship had developed into a committed relationship.
History questions assessed the total number of situationships experienced, concurrent involvement, the maximum number experienced concurrently, and returning to a previous situationship.
Open-ended questions invited explanations of concurrency and returning.

Several bespoke items were developed for the broader project (see Supplementary Table S2), informed by research on casual relationships and recurring themes in the limited qualitative and popular accounts of situationships, including ambiguity, mixed signals, uncertain progression, and uneven expectations.
text.formatted: Several bespoke items were developed for the broader project (see Supplementary Table <ref type="table" target="#tab_1">S2</ref>), informed by research on casual relationships and recurring themes in the limited qualitative and popular accounts of situationships, including ambiguity, mixed signals, uncertain progression, and uneven expectations.

text.text: Items were rated from 1 (strongly disagree) to 5 (strongly agree), with N/A available.
Four items assessed anticipated long-term potential, hoped-for relationship progression, loneliness or a need for connection, and evaluation of long-term compatibility.
Two further items assessed assumed sexual exclusivity without defining the relationship and anticipated betrayal if the partner was seeing other people.
An open-ended question asked whether exclusivity had been discussed and whether a clear mutual understanding had been reached.
Participants completed the nine-item Sociosexual Orientation Inventory-Revised (SOI-R; Penke & Asendorpf, 2008), assessing sexual behaviour, attitudes towards uncommitted sex, and sociosexual desire.
text.formatted: Participants completed the nine-item Sociosexual Orientation Inventory-Revised (SOI-R; <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Penke & Asendorpf, 2008)</ref>, assessing sexual behaviour, attitudes towards uncommitted sex, and sociosexual desire.

text.text: Each component comprises three items with nine response categories; higher scores indicate more unrestricted sociosexuality.
Item 6 was reverse-scored, and component and global scores were calculated as means of available items; one participant omitted one desire item.
Internal consistency was acceptable to good for behaviour (α = .76), attitudes (α = .84), desire (α = .81), and the global scale (α = .83).
Scores were contextualised using sex-specific means and standard deviations from Penke and Asendorpf's (2008) large reference sample (Study 1).
text.formatted: Scores were contextualised using sex-specific means and standard deviations from <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">Penke and Asendorpf's (2008)</ref> large reference sample (Study 1).

text.text: After providing informed consent, participants completed demographic and relationship questions.
They described their current situationship or, if not currently involved in one, their most emotionally significant past situationship.

Participants describing past situationships answered experience items with reference to their feelings during or after the relationship, whereas those describing ongoing situationships reported their current feelings.
Separate questions concerned their wider relationship histories.

Participants then completed the situationship-characteristics checklist, ratings of motivations and exclusivity expectations, an attention-check item ("This is an attention check, pick 2."), the SOI-R, and open-ended questions about their experiences.
Finally, they received a written debrief.
Categorical responses were summarised as counts and percentages using valid denominators, and rating items and SOI-R scores as means and standard deviations.
Checklist selections were non-mutually exclusive.
Free-text meeting responses were manually categorised.
A past situationship was counted as having transitioned whenever the participant answered yes to "Did it lead to a committed relationship?", even if the subsequent relationship had ended.
Current experiences were identified using the separate status item, coded as ongoing, and excluded from transition percentages.
Past durations represent completed lengths, whereas current durations represent elapsed lengths.
Exploratory sex comparisons were conducted for the 12 coded definitional attributes and the 10 checklist statements using odds ratios, 95% Wald confidence intervals, and two-sided Wald tests.
The four motivation and two exclusivity items were compared using two-sided Welch independent-samples t tests with Hedges' g (Hedges, 1981).

text.text: Benjamini-Hochberg corrections (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) were applied to each family of comparisons.

text.text: For descriptive endorsement percentages, ratings of 4-5 were treated as agreement and ratings of 1-3 as non-agreement.
SOI-R means were compared with published sex-specific reference values using two-sided Welch tests calculated from summary statistics, with Hedges' g as the effect size.
Holm correction (Holm, 1979) was retained across the eight benchmark comparisons.

text.text: Formation and course comparisons used odds ratios for binary responses and χ² tests for responses with more than two categories, with Benjamini-Hochberg correction across the 12 comparisons.

Two-sided binomial tests compared male initiation with 50% overall and separately within women's and men's reports, with Holm correction across the three tests.

The qualitative coding plan used structured content coding informed by act-nomination procedures, with recurring attributes derived inductively from participants' responses (Buss & Craik, 1983; Hsieh & Shannon, 2005).

text.text: Relationship-oriented motives were common at the aggregate level.
In total 55.6% agreed or strongly agreed that they had entered hoping the situationship would lead to a relationship.
Overall, 54.7% assumed sexual exclusivity.
Responses to assumed sexual exclusivity were divided in both sexes: 56.8% of women and 50.4% of men agreed that they had assumed exclusivity, whereas 31.3% and 37.8%, respectively, disagreed.
Only 11.9% of women and 11.8% of men selected the neutral midpoint.
Most women (68.2%) and men (58.1%) also agreed that they would feel betrayed if their partner was seeing other people.

text.text: The present study provides, to our knowledge, the largest quantitative examination of situationships to date.
The study extended earlier research beyond predominantly student samples (e.g., Langlais et al., 2024), drawing on a broader range of adult perspectives and relationship histories.
text.formatted: The study extended earlier research beyond predominantly student samples (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Langlais et al., 2024)</ref>, drawing on a broader range of adult perspectives and relationship histories.

text.text: Analyses yielded a working empirical definition of situationships and identified sex differences in participants' understandings and expectations, alongside contrasting patterns across behavioural and attitudinal components of sociosexuality.

Our analyses informed a working definition of situationships as intimate, relationshiplike connections lacking clearly established levels of commitment or a mutually recognised relationship status, often accompanied by uncertainty about their future trajectory.
Their recurring, relationship-like nature distinguishes them conceptually from one-night stands and isolated hookups (Wentland & Reissing, 2014).
text.formatted: Their recurring, relationship-like nature distinguishes them conceptually from one-night stands and isolated hookups <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Wentland & Reissing, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: They share ongoing intimacy with friends-with-benefits relationships (Bisson & Levine, 2009), but the working definition foregrounds unresolved questions about status and trajectory.
text.formatted: They share ongoing intimacy with friends-with-benefits relationships <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bisson & Levine, 2009)</ref>, but the working definition foregrounds unresolved questions about status and trajectory.

text.text: An explicitly understood friendswith-benefits arrangement may therefore resemble a situationship behaviourally while differing in the clarity of relational expectations.
Women more often emphasised ambiguity in their definitions and endorsed the statement "There's emotional confusion, not just sexual casualness" more frequently than men (62.3% vs.
Together with women's stronger hopes for commitment, this suggests that men in our sample approached situationships more casually, whereas women perceived greater potential for long-term commitment.

This pattern is consistent with Sexual Strategies Theory (Buss & Schmitt, 1993), which links men's stronger short-term mating orientation to potential reproductive gains from additional partners, and women's greater emphasis on commitment to their higher obligatory parental investment (Trivers, 1972).
text.formatted: This pattern is consistent with Sexual Strategies Theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Buss & Schmitt, 1993)</ref>, which links men's stronger short-term mating orientation to potential reproductive gains from additional partners, and women's greater emphasis on commitment to their higher obligatory parental investment <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Trivers, 1972)</ref>.

text.text: Situationships may create scope for sexual conflict when men seek continued sexual involvement without commitment while women hope for progression to a committed relationship (Buss, 2017).
text.formatted: Situationships may create scope for sexual conflict when men seek continued sexual involvement without commitment while women hope for progression to a committed relationship <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Buss, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Ambiguity may sustain these connections by allowing intimacy to continue without explicitly acknowledging or resolving competing expectations.
Women more strongly endorsed feeling they would be betrayed if their situationship partner was seeing others, although assumed exclusivity did not differ significantly by sex.
For some, discovering non-exclusivity may threaten both an assumed arrangement and hopes for commitment.
More broadly, hopes for progression and assumptions of exclusivity show that undefined relationships can carry substantial relational expectations.
The uncertainty may concern whether those expectations are recognised and shared.
The sociosexuality findings illustrate the importance of distinguishing sexual behaviour from attitudes towards uncommitted sex.
Compared with the reference sample (Penke & Asendorpf, 2008), both sexes reported higher behavioural sociosexuality scores, whereas women reported more restricted attitudes.
text.formatted: Compared with the reference sample <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Penke & Asendorpf, 2008)</ref>, both sexes reported higher behavioural sociosexuality scores, whereas women reported more restricted attitudes.

text.text: This pattern raises questions about potential incongruence between women's sexual experiences and preferences.
One possibility is that some women pursue a short-term for long-term mating strategy in the hope of securing commitment (Greiling & Buss, 2000).
text.formatted: One possibility is that some women pursue a short-term for long-term mating strategy in the hope of securing commitment <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Greiling & Buss, 2000)</ref>.

text.text: Yet in this sample, only 9% of reported past situationships progressed to committed relationships, which might suggest that such a strategy is not effective in contemporary mating ecologies.
Dating apps were the most common meeting context in our sample.

Online daters often pursue partners more desirable than themselves (Bruch & Newman, 2018), and men report lower minimum standards for short-term sexual partners than for long-term partners (Kenrick et al., 1990; Kenrick et al., 1993).
text.formatted: Online daters often pursue partners more desirable than themselves <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bruch & Newman, 2018)</ref>, and men report lower minimum standards for short-term sexual partners than for long-term partners <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Kenrick et al., 1990;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Kenrick et al., 1993)</ref>.

text.text: Sexual intimacy with a desirable man, therefore, may not imply comparable prospects for commitment.
Women in our sample perceived greater long-term potential in their partners than men did, and some may interpret continued sexual intimacy as evidence that their long-term interest is reciprocated.
Women's expectations of commitment may also be sustained by deception.
Sexual conflict research reviewed by Buss (2017) found that 71% of men in the sample reported exaggerating their feelings to obtain sex.
text.formatted: Sexual conflict research reviewed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Buss (2017)</ref> found that 71% of men in the sample reported exaggerating their feelings to obtain sex.

text.text: Misleading expressions of emotional investment may therefore encourage some women to enter or remain in situationships expecting eventual commitment.
Repeated situationship involvement was common among women (63%) and men (62%).
Alongside women's stronger hopes for progression, this suggests that repeated involvement need not reflect a preference for uncommitted relationships.
For some women, successive situationships could represent repeated attempts to find a partner willing to commit, potentially sustained by misleading expressions of investment.
Women's number of sexual partners, colloquially termed "body count" (Thomas et al., 2025), could therefore increase despite relatively restricted attitudes towards uncommitted sex.
text.formatted: Women's number of sexual partners, colloquially termed "body count" <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Thomas et al., 2025)</ref>, could therefore increase despite relatively restricted attitudes towards uncommitted sex.

text.text: Returning to a previous situationship, reported by 53% of women and 43% of men, may similarly reflect renewed hopes for progression.

That roughly 42% of past and ongoing situationships had lasted at least seven months also raises the possibility that hopes for commitment sustain prolonged involvement despite unresolved expectations.

Future research should examine whether unsuccessful attempts to secure commitment, sexual deception, or misperceptions of partners' intentions contribute to potential incongruence between women's sociosexual behaviour and attitudes, and whether such incongruence is associated with lower wellbeing or satisfaction.

Writing in TIME magazine, sex and dating coach Myisha Battle (2023) argued that situationships can offer intimacy and flexibility without pressure to define the relationship or progress towards commitment.
In light of our findings, however, these potential benefits may not be shared equally between men and women.
Continued participation does not establish that both partners welcome ambiguity or share expectations.
Hopes for commitment and assumptions of exclusivity may remain unspoken.
Research on consensual non-monogamy identifies disclosure and open communication as relationship-maintenance practices (Mogilski et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Research on consensual non-monogamy identifies disclosure and open communication as relationship-maintenance practices <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Mogilski et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Yet ambiguity may sustain situationships when partners want different outcomes, potentially benefiting one more than the other.
This possibility requires dyadic research involving both partners.
Relationship difficulties are among the most frequently reported concerns brought to counselling (National Counselling and Psychotherapy Society, 2026).
text.formatted: Relationship difficulties are among the most frequently reported concerns brought to counselling <ref type="bibr">(National Counselling and Psychotherapy Society, 2026)</ref>.

text.text: When someone raises a situationship in individual counselling, a useful starting point may be to distinguish what they hope for or assume from what their partner has actually communicated, and to explore whether attempts to clarify commitment, exclusivity, or future intentions have been avoided.
Most participants reported on a past situationship, so their recollections of earlier feelings and expectations may have been influenced by how it ended.
Asking participants to describe their most emotionally significant experience may also have captured experiences that were not typical of their situationships more generally.
Following situationships over time would help clarify how expectations develop and whether accounts change once the outcome is known.
We did not recruit matched comparison groups from other relationship types, so we cannot establish whether the patterns observed are specific to situationships.
Published SOI-R values (Penke & Asendorpf, 2008) provided a useful benchmark, but differences in sample composition and recruitment may partly explain the differences in scores.
text.formatted: Published SOI-R values <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Penke & Asendorpf, 2008)</ref> provided a useful benchmark, but differences in sample composition and recruitment may partly explain the differences in scores.

text.text: Future research should directly compare situationships with committed relationships, casual dating, and friends-withbenefits arrangements to establish which characteristics and sociosexuality patterns distinguish them.

Given the observed sex differences, sexual conflict theory (Buss, 2017) offers a useful theoretical framework for investigating whether divergent mating goals produce unequal benefits and costs within situationships.
text.formatted: Given the observed sex differences, sexual conflict theory <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Buss, 2017)</ref> offers a useful theoretical framework for investigating whether divergent mating goals produce unequal benefits and costs within situationships.

text.text: Sex differences in sexual regret, particularly evidence linking women's more restricted sociosexual attitudes to greater regret, warrant investigation given the potential sociosexuality incongruence identified here (Galperin et al., 2013; Kennair et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Sex differences in sexual regret, particularly evidence linking women's more restricted sociosexual attitudes to greater regret, warrant investigation given the potential sociosexuality incongruence identified here <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Galperin et al., 2013;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">Kennair et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Future research should also investigate whether situationships shape subsequent attitudes towards commitment, expectations of partners, and relationship satisfaction.
One hypothesis is that sexual involvement with a man perceived as higher in mate value who is unwilling to commit may establish a comparison standard for subsequent partners.
This could reduce satisfaction with partners perceived as less desirable, even when they offer the commitment previously sought.
Examining this possibility would clarify whether situationships' consequences extend beyond the connections themselves.
This study provided a working empirical definition of situationships and identified sex differences in how they were understood and experienced.

Hopes for commitment and assumptions of exclusivity, despite infrequent progression to committed relationships, suggest that involvement in an undefined relationship need not reflect a preference for remaining uncommitted.
Research informed by sexual conflict theory can test how partners' goals interact over time and shape these connections' costs and benefits.
